baseline_rows.pred_answer: High-risk. The system is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by the Medical Device Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) listed in Annex I, and that device must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk. Under Article 43(3) the provider follows the Medical Device Regulation's conformity assessment procedure with a notified body, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, yielding a single CE marking. The provider must therefore meet the risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), logging (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), accuracy and cybersecurity (Article 15), and quality management system (Article 17) obligations as part of the medical-device conformity assessment.

Not always. Article 6(2) classifies an Annex III system as high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs one of four tasks: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of the Article 6(3) conditions. The provider relying on this derogation must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that evaluates or classifies natural persons or groups of persons over a period of time based on their social behaviour or personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to either or both of detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected, and treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. This prohibition binds any provider or deployer, public or private.

Not prohibited. Article 5 prohibits biometric categorisation only where it deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and emotion recognition is prohibited only in the workplace and in education institutions except for medical or safety reasons. A therapy setting is neither a workplace nor an education institution, so emotion recognition there is not prohibited by Article 5.
I am Lexy, a Compliance assistant that can answer your questions related to the EU AI Act, based on my Knowledge Graph and ontology. What can I help you with?

Not high-risk. A translation AI system is not listed among the Annex III use cases, which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk, and it is not typically a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, which is the Article 6(1) route to high-risk classification. It is limited risk, carrying the Article 50(1) transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons, unless that interaction is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.

The provider must draw up technical documentation before placing the system on the market, containing at a minimum the elements set out in Annex IV, which include a general description of the system, a detailed description of the elements of the system and of the process for its development, detailed information about monitoring, functioning and control (including capabilities, limitations, performance metrics, foreseeable risks, and human oversight measures), a description of the risk management system, the data governance and management practices, the technical specifications, the validation and testing procedures, and a description of the post-market monitoring system. Article 11 requires the documentation to demonstrate compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and to be kept up to date. An SME may provide the Annex IV elements in simplified form using the Commission's targeted form.

Article 50(1) sets the transparency obligation for a patient-facing medical chatbot. The provider must design the system so that the natural person is informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the chatbot generates synthetic content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The prohibition applies to untargeted scraping regardless of the database's structure or duration, while targeted scraping of specific individuals remains permitted.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or group by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits systems that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

The seven guiding principles of the EU AI Act are articulated in Recital 27 (the trustworthy-AI framework) and inform the human-centric purpose of Article 1: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; social and environmental wellbeing; and accountability. Article 4 operationalises these principles by requiring providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff.

The provider must submit the information listed in Annex VIII Section A when registering a high-risk AI system under Article 49(1). That information comprises the name, address and contact details of the provider; where another person submits on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the AI system (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that notified body where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable; any Member States in which the AI system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; electronic instructions for use (except for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7); and optionally a URL for additional information.

Not high-risk and not prohibited. A spam filter does not fall within any of the eight prohibited practices listed in Article 5, nor is it a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), nor does it match any of the Annex III use cases classified as high-risk under Article 6(2). It is therefore limited risk, carrying the Article 50(1) transparency duty only where it interacts directly with natural persons and that interaction is not obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

An AI opponent in a video game is not regulated under the EU AI Act. The system does not fall within any of the eight prohibited practices listed in Article 5, nor does it meet either of the two high-risk routes established by Article 6: it is not a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, and it does not perform any of the Annex III use cases such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential public services, law enforcement, migration or administration of justice. The system carries no obligations beyond the Article 50(1) transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons, requiring the provider to design it so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system.

High-risk is defined on two cumulative conditions under Article 6(1), or by falling within Annex III under Article 6(2). Article 6(1) makes a system high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Article 6(3) permits an Annex III system to escape high-risk classification only where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs one of four narrow tasks, unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk.

The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

Not high-risk unless it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk. A customer service chatbot does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so it is not high-risk under Article 6(2). It carries the Article 50(1) transparency duty: the provider must design it so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person taking into account the circumstances and context of use.

A notified body must be involved where the high-risk AI medical device is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the medical device legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Article 43(3) integrates the EU AI Act conformity assessment into the medical device regulation's own notified-body procedure, yielding a single assessment covering both regimes. The notified body examines the technical documentation, audits the quality management system, and may require access to training and validation data sets, issuing a Union technical documentation assessment certificate where the system conforms to the Chapter III Section 2 requirements.

No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

High-risk. Article 6(2) classifies AI systems referred to in Annex III as high-risk, and Annex III(4) lists employment, workers management and access to self-employment as a high-risk use-case category, which includes recruitment and hiring systems that evaluate candidates for hiring or promotion decisions.

The system is high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices) and that medical device must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Where those conditions hold, the provider follows the medical device legislation's own conformity assessment procedure, and the EU AI Act requirements form part of that assessment.

Article 14 governs human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems. It requires that such systems be designed and developed with capabilities enabling natural persons to whom oversight is assigned to understand the system's capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output, and intervene in the operation of the system or interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure. The deployer's duty to assign competent natural persons to carry out that oversight is set out in Article 26(2).

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or group by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits exploiting vulnerabilities of a natural person or specific group due to their age, disability or specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace, except where the use is intended for medical or safety reasons. The medical or safety carve-out is narrow and must be the system's primary purpose at market placement, such as fatigue detection in pilots or drivers for accident prevention. Using emotion recognition to improve manufacturing efficiency does not fall within that carve-out, so the practice is prohibited.

No. Article 2(6) excludes AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. A biomedical research system that operates solely within that research context and is not placed on the market falls outside the Regulation's scope.

Not high-risk. An AI image generator is not listed in Annex III and is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I legislation, so it does not meet either route to high-risk classification under Article 6. The provider must mark the synthetic images in a machine-readable format as artificially generated under Article 50(2), unless the system performs only assistive standard editing that does not substantially alter the input or its semantics.

Not high-risk. An AI system that schedules administrative appointments in a clinic is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, which is the first route to high-risk classification under Article 6(1), and it does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. The system is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.

Not high-risk. An AI inventory-management tool is not listed in Annex III and is not a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, so it does not meet either route to high-risk classification under Article 6. It is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Article 9(2) establishes the risk assessment criteria for high-risk AI systems: the provider must identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse. Article 7(2) sets the criteria the Commission applies when assessing whether to add, modify or remove a use case in Annex III: the intended purpose of the system, the extent to which it has been or is likely to be used, the nature and amount of data processed (including special categories of personal data), the extent to which the system acts autonomously and the possibility for a human to override it, the extent to which use has already caused harm or adverse impact on fundamental rights, and the potential extent of such harm in terms of intensity and ability to affect multiple persons or disproportionately affect a particular group. Article 9(4) requires risk management measures to give due consideration to the effects and interactions of the combined requirements with a view to minimising risks whilst achieving an appropriate balance, and Article 9(5) requires testing to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures.

Not high-risk. A consumer wellness chatbot that gives general lifestyle tips and makes no medical claims falls outside both high-risk routes: it is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and it does not fall within any of the eight Annex III use cases. It is minimal risk, carrying no Chapter III obligations and no Article 50 transparency duty unless it qualifies as a general-purpose AI model under Article 51.

Not high-risk. A music recommendation system is not a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, nor does it fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so Article 6 does not classify it as high-risk. It is limited risk, carrying the Article 50(1) transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons, requiring the provider to design the system so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious from the circumstances.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons (Article 26(2)), monitor the operation of the system on the basis of the instructions for use and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and keep the logs automatically generated by the system to the extent such logs are under their control (Article 26(7)). Deployers that are employers must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the high-risk system into service (Article 26(7)). Deployers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human-oversight measures and complaints workflows (Article 27). Financial institutions subject to Union financial-services internal-governance requirements fulfil the monitoring and log-retention obligations by complying with the governance arrangements under that financial-services law (Article 26(5) and Article 26(6)).

Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

Article 17(1) requires the quality management system to include a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system; techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the system; techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the system; and examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they must be carried out. The system must be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions. Article 63(1) permits microenterprises to comply with certain elements of the quality management system in a simplified manner, provided they do not have partner or linked enterprises, without affecting the level of protection or compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

Article 53(1) requires the provider to maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream-provider information per Annex XII, implement a copyright policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training data. Where the model is made available in a system that interacts directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) requires the provider to design the system so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the model generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated.

The AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1), not "medium risk." Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Medical devices are listed in Annex I, so the AI system meets both conditions and is therefore high-risk. Under Article 43(3), the provider follows the medical device legislation's own conformity assessment procedure, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that single assessment.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27). A person subject to a deployer decision based on the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects health, safety or fundamental rights has a right to an explanation (Article 86). These are deployer duties only: the hospital does not bear the provider's design and conformity duties unless it becomes a provider under Article 25 by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing the intended purpose.

This question is about the Digital Services Act (DSA), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the applicable rules.

Article 50(1) requires providers to design AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so they are informed they are interacting with AI, unless this is obvious. Article 50(2) requires providers of generative AI to mark synthetic audio, image, video, or text in a machine-readable, detectable format. Article 50(3) requires deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems to inform exposed natural persons of their operation.

Not high-risk. The system does not fall within the Annex I route under Article 6(1) because a transcription-only ambient scribe is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. It does not fall within the Annex III route under Article 6(2) because pure transcription of consultations is not among the eight high-risk use cases, and in particular it is not the evaluation of eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare under Annex III(5)(a), which covers eligibility assessment rather than documentation. The system is therefore limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Yes. An AI system intended as a safety component of a robotic surgical device is high-risk under Article 6(1) because a surgical robot is a Class IIb or Class III medical device requiring notified-body conformity assessment under Article 43. Since the AI operates in a real-time control loop, Article 14 requires robust human oversight measures to allow the surgeon to override or reverse decisions. Under Article 72 and Article 73, the provider must establish post-market monitoring and report serious incidents, coordinating with the Medical Device Regulation Article 83 for layered surveillance.

This question is about the Digital Services Act (DSA), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the applicable rules.

A provider (Article 3(3)) develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity, so the provider bears the design and conformity duties of Article 16 while the deployer bears the use-phase duties of Article 26. Under Article 25 a deployer, distributor, importer, or other third party becomes a provider, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system, or modifies a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that infers or identifies emotions of natural persons in the workplace and in education institutions, with a narrow exception for systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons. Article 50(3) requires deployers of an emotion recognition system to inform the natural persons exposed to it of the system's operation, except where the system is permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences. Outside the workplace and education settings emotion recognition is not prohibited, and where such a system interacts directly with natural persons the provider must design it to inform them they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1).

A conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system consists of verifying that the quality management system complies with Article 17, examining the technical documentation to assess compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and verifying that the design, development process and post-market monitoring plan are consistent with the technical documentation, as set out in Annex VI for the internal-control procedure. Where the provider has not applied harmonised standards or common specifications in full, the assessment under Annex VII adds notified-body involvement: the notified body audits the quality management system, examines the technical documentation, and issues an EU technical documentation assessment certificate. For a high-risk system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation, Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into that legislation's own third-party conformity assessment procedure as a single combined assessment.

Article 10 requires the provider to establish data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, ensuring that training, validation and testing datasets are relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete. The provider must examine the data for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, and may process special categories of personal data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction. The technical documentation under Article 11 and Annex IV must describe the data requirements, including datasheets on training methodologies, provenance, scope, main characteristics, how the data was obtained and selected, labelling procedures, and data cleaning methodologies. A high-risk system trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used is presumed to comply with the Article 10(4) data governance requirements under Article 42(1).

Non-compliance with the Article 50 transparency obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(4)(g). Article 50 imposes transparency duties split by actor: providers must ensure AI systems interacting with natural persons disclose their AI nature (Article 50(1)) and must mark synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable format (Article 50(2)), while deployers must inform exposed persons when operating emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems (Article 50(3)) and must label deepfakes as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs including start-ups, the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount.

It's difficult to name a single "best" restaurant in Rome, as it truly depends on your personal taste, budget, and the type of cuisine you're looking for! Rome offers an incredible variety of dining experiences, from traditional trattorias serving classic Roman dishes to Michelin-starred establishments.

Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

Article 20(1) requires the provider to take the necessary corrective actions immediately to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it, or recall it, as appropriate, once the provider considers or has reason to consider the system is not in conformity. The Regulation does not specify a timeframe within which the market surveillance authority must allow corrective action before requiring suspension or recall, so the provider's duty to act without undue delay arises as soon as it has reason to consider non-conformity, including when the authority determines the system is high-risk. Where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 20(2) requires the provider to immediately investigate the causes and inform the market surveillance authorities and any notified body that issued a certificate. The gravity of the situation determines which corrective action is appropriate under Article 20(1), but the duty to act immediately applies in all cases of non-conformity.

A risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain.

Not automatically. Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

Article 5 prohibits eight AI practices outright: subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or socio-economic situation, social scoring leading to unjustified detrimental treatment, criminal-offence risk profiling of natural persons, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial-recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace or educational institutions, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement subject to the narrow Article 5(1)(h) exceptions.

The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

Not prohibited and not high-risk under the Annex III use cases. Article 5 prohibits eight categories of AI practice, none of which covers medical transcription. Annex III(5)(d) classifies emergency patient triage systems as high-risk but does not list transcription of doctor-patient conversations. The transcription system is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk.

No, the Regulation does not require market surveillance authorities to be provided with remote access to documentation and datasets. Article 16(k) requires the provider to demonstrate conformity upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, and Article 26 requires deployers to cooperate with market surveillance authorities, but neither provision mandates remote access. The provider keeps the technical documentation for ten years after placing the system on the market (Article 18), and the datasets used to develop the system form part of that documentation under Article 11 and Annex IV, but the Act specifies no particular means of access.

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

High-risk only where the software is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Article 6(1) classifies a system as high-risk on those two cumulative conditions. Melanoma-detection software deployed as part of a medical device regulated under the Medical Device Regulation or In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Device Regulation would meet this route where the device itself requires third-party conformity assessment by a notified body. Article 43(3) then requires the provider to follow the conformity assessment procedure of that sectoral legislation, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

Not high-risk and not prohibited under the facts stated. Article 5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation only where it deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, so sorting patients by biometric data for trial eligibility does not engage that prohibition unless the system infers one of those protected attributes. The system is high-risk only where it falls within an Annex III use case, and selecting patients for an experimental clinical trial is not among them: Annex III(5)(a) covers evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare, by or on behalf of public authorities, which does not reach a hospital's internal trial-selection process, and Annex III(5)(d) covers emergency patient triage, dispatch or priority-setting of emergency first response services, which does not extend to non-emergency research enrolment. Absent a listed use case the system is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Yes, where the device is high-risk. A provider of a high-risk AI system must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the system (Article 72(1)), actively and systematically collecting, documenting and analysing relevant data to evaluate continuous compliance with Chapter III Section 2 requirements (Article 72(2)), based on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation under Annex IV (Article 72(3)). The provider must report any serious incident to the market-surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred (Article 73(1)), immediately after establishing a causal link and not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident (Article 73(2)). For a device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation, Article 72(4) integrates the post-market monitoring elements into the post-market surveillance system and plan already established under that legislation, and Article 73(10) limits the AI Act reporting duty to serious incidents involving an infringement of Union law protecting fundamental rights.

For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

No. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases at the time of classification, and a system that no longer performs an Annex III use case is not high-risk under that route. The classification turns on the system's current intended purpose as specified in the instructions for use, promotional materials and technical documentation (Article 3(12)), not on what it previously did.

Article 10(2)(f) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to examine training, validation and testing datasets for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination. Article 10(5) permits providers to process special categories of personal data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards, technical limitations on re-use, and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures including pseudonymisation. Article 9 requires the risk management system to be documented and to identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimate and evaluate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and adopt targeted risk management measures that give due consideration to the combined application of the Chapter III Section 2 requirements. For general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, Article 55(1)(a) requires providers to perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks, and Article 55(1)(b) requires them to assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources.

No. Article 15(1) requires the provider to design and develop the high-risk system so that it achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and performs consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle. Article 9(1) requires a documented risk management system that is maintained in relation to the high-risk AI system, and Article 17(1) requires a quality management system that includes examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development. The lifecycle obligation means the provider must continue to ensure those levels are maintained, not merely confirm them once at development.

branch_rows.pred_answer: High-risk. The system is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by the Medical Device Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) listed in Annex I, and that device must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk. Under Article 43(3) the provider follows the Medical Device Regulation's conformity assessment procedure with a notified body, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, yielding a single CE marking. The provider must therefore implement a risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), logging (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), accuracy and cybersecurity (Article 15), and a quality management system (Article 17), all assessed through the notified-body route under the medical-device legislation.

Not always. Article 6(2) classifies an Annex III system as high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs one of four tasks: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of the Article 6(3) conditions. The provider relying on this derogation must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that evaluates or classifies natural persons or groups of persons over a period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to either or both of detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected, and treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. This prohibition binds any provider or deployer, public or private.

Not prohibited. Article 5 prohibits biometric categorisation only where it deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and emotion recognition is prohibited only in the workplace and in education institutions except for medical or safety reasons. A therapy setting is neither a workplace nor an education institution, so emotion recognition there is not prohibited by Article 5.
I am Lexy, a Compliance assistant that can answer your questions related to the EU AI Act, based on my Knowledge Graph and ontology. What can I help you with?

Not high-risk. A translation AI system is not listed among the Annex III use cases, which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk, and it is not typically a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, which is the Article 6(1) route to high-risk classification. It carries the Article 50(1) transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons, unless that interaction is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person taking into account the circumstances and context of use.

The provider must draw up technical documentation before placing the system on the market, containing at a minimum the elements set out in Annex IV, which include a general description of the system, a detailed description of the elements of the system and of the process for its development, detailed information about monitoring, functioning and control (including capabilities, limitations, performance metrics, foreseeable risks, and human oversight measures), a description of the risk management system, the data governance and management practices, the technical specifications, the validation and testing procedures, and a description of the post-market monitoring system. Article 11 requires the documentation to demonstrate compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and to be kept up to date. An SME may provide the Annex IV elements in simplified form using the Commission's targeted form.

Article 50(1) sets the transparency obligation for a patient-facing medical chatbot. The provider must design the system so that the natural person is informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the chatbot generates synthetic content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The prohibition applies to untargeted scraping regardless of the database's structure or duration, while targeted scraping of specific individuals remains permitted.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or group by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits systems that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

The seven guiding principles of the EU AI Act are articulated in Recital 27 (the trustworthy-AI framework) and inform the human-centric purpose of Article 1: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; social and environmental wellbeing; and accountability. Article 4 operationalises these principles by requiring providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff.

The provider must submit the information listed in Annex VIII Section A when registering a high-risk AI system under Article 49(1). That information comprises the name, address and contact details of the provider; where another person submits on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions the system supports; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the AI system (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that notified body where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable; any Member States in which the AI system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; electronic instructions for use, except for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7; and optionally a URL for additional information.

Not high-risk and not prohibited. A spam filter does not fall within any of the eight prohibited practices listed in Article 5, nor is it a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), nor does it match any of the Annex III use cases classified as high-risk under Article 6(2). It is therefore limited risk, carrying the Article 50(1) transparency duty only where it interacts directly with natural persons and that interaction is not obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

An AI opponent in a video game is not regulated under the EU AI Act. The system does not fall within any of the eight prohibited practices listed in Article 5, nor does it meet either of the two high-risk routes established by Article 6: it is not a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, and it does not perform any of the Annex III use cases such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential public services, law enforcement, migration or administration of justice. The system carries no obligations under the Act unless it interacts directly with natural persons in a way that triggers the Article 50(1) transparency duty to disclose its AI nature, which would not apply to an opponent character whose artificial nature is evident from the game context.

High-risk is defined on two cumulative conditions under Article 6(1), or by falling within Annex III under Article 6(2). Article 6(1) makes a system high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. An Annex III system escapes high-risk under Article 6(3) only where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs one of four narrow tasks, unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk.

The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

Not high-risk unless it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), which is unlikely for a customer service chatbot. A customer service chatbot does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, which cover biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. The provider must design the system so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1), unless that is obvious from the circumstances and context of use.

A notified body must be involved where the high-risk AI medical device is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the medical device legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Article 43(3) integrates the EU AI Act conformity assessment into the medical device regulation's own notified-body procedure, yielding a single assessment covering both regimes. The notified body examines the technical documentation, audits the quality management system, and may require access to training and validation data sets, issuing a Union technical documentation assessment certificate where the system conforms to the Chapter III Section 2 requirements.

No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

High-risk. Article 6(2) classifies AI systems referred to in Annex III as high-risk, and Annex III(4) lists employment, workers management and access to self-employment as a high-risk use-case category, which includes recruitment and hiring systems that evaluate candidates for hiring or promotion decisions.

The system is high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that device must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the medical device regulation. Under Article 2(2) only Article 6(1), Articles 102 to 109 and Article 112 apply to such systems, so the full Chapter III Section 2 requirements do not apply and the provider follows the medical device legislation's own conformity assessment procedure with the EU AI Act requirements integrated into that assessment.

Article 14 governs human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems. It requires that such systems be designed and developed with capabilities enabling natural persons to whom oversight is assigned to understand the system's capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output, and intervene in the operation of the system or interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure. The deployer's duty to assign competent natural persons to carry out that oversight is set out in Article 26(2).

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or group by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not have otherwise taken in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Article 5(1)(b) separately prohibits systems that exploit vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

Prohibited. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace, except where the use is intended for medical or safety reasons. The medical or safety carve-out is narrow and must be the system's primary purpose at market placement, such as fatigue detection in pilots or drivers for accident prevention, not a post-hoc efficiency justification. Monitoring manufacturing workers' emotions and stress levels to improve efficiency does not fall within that carve-out and is therefore a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(f).

No. Article 2(6) excludes AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. A biomedical research system that is not placed on the market falls outside the Regulation's scope under this exclusion.

Not high-risk. An AI image generator is not listed in Annex III and is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I harmonisation legislation, so it does not meet either route to high-risk classification under Article 6. The provider must mark the synthetic image outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated under Article 50(2), unless the system performs only assistive standard editing that does not substantially alter the input data.

Not high-risk. An AI system that schedules administrative appointments in a clinic is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, which is the first route to high-risk classification under Article 6(1), and it does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. The system is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.

Not high-risk. An AI inventory-management tool is not listed in Annex III and is not a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, so it does not meet either route to high-risk classification under Article 6. It is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Article 9(2) establishes the risk assessment criteria for high-risk AI systems: the provider must identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse. Article 7(2) sets the criteria the Commission applies when assessing whether to add, modify or remove a use case in Annex III: the intended purpose of the system, the extent to which it has been or is likely to be used, the nature and amount of data processed (including special categories of personal data), the extent to which the system acts autonomously and the possibility for a human to override its output, the extent to which use has already caused harm or adverse impact on fundamental rights, and the potential extent of such harm in terms of intensity and ability to affect multiple persons or disproportionately affect a particular group. Article 9(4) requires risk management measures to give due consideration to the effects and interactions of the combined requirements with a view to minimising risks whilst achieving an appropriate balance, and Article 9(5) requires testing to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures.

Not high-risk. A consumer wellness chatbot that gives general lifestyle tips and makes no medical claims falls outside both high-risk routes: it is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and it does not fall within any of the eight Annex III use cases. It is therefore minimal risk, carrying no Chapter III obligations and no Article 50 transparency duty unless it qualifies as a general-purpose AI model under Article 51.

Not high-risk. A music recommendation system is not a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, nor does it fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so Article 6 does not classify it as high-risk. It is limited risk, carrying the Article 50(1) transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons, requiring the provider to design the system so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious from the circumstances.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons (Article 26(2)), monitor the operation of the system on the basis of the instructions for use and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and keep the logs automatically generated by the system to the extent such logs are under their control (Article 26(7)). Deployers that are employers must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the high-risk system into service (Article 26(7)). Deployers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the deployment process, affected persons, specific risks, human-oversight measures and complaints workflows (Article 27). Financial institutions subject to Union financial-services internal-governance requirements fulfil the monitoring and log-retention obligations by complying with the governance arrangements under that financial-services law (Article 26(5) and Article 26(6)).

Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

Article 17(1) requires the quality management system to include a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the high-risk AI system; techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the system; techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the system; and examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they must be carried out. The system must be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions. Article 63(1) permits microenterprises to comply with certain elements of the quality management system in a simplified manner, provided they do not have partner or linked enterprises, without affecting the level of protection or compliance with the Section 2 requirements.

Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

Article 53(1) requires the provider to maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream-provider information per Annex XII, implement a copyright policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training data. Where the model is made available in a system that interacts directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) requires the provider to design the system so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system. Where the model generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated.

The AI system is high-risk under Article 6(1), not "medium risk." Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Medical devices are listed in Annex I, so the AI system meets both conditions and is therefore high-risk. Under Article 43(3), the provider follows the medical device legislation's own conformity assessment procedure, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that single assessment.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27). A person subject to a deployer decision based on the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects health, safety or fundamental rights has a right to an explanation (Article 86). These are deployer duties only: the hospital does not bear the provider's design and conformity duties unless it becomes a provider under Article 25 by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing the intended purpose.

This question is about the Digital Services Act (DSA), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the applicable rules.

Article 50(1) requires providers to design AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so they are informed they are interacting with AI, unless this is obvious. Article 50(2) requires providers of generative AI to mark synthetic audio, image, video, or text in a machine-readable, detectable format. Article 50(3) requires deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems to inform exposed natural persons of their operation.

Not high-risk. The system does not fall within the Annex I route under Article 6(1) because a transcription-only scribe is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. It does not fall within the Annex III route under Article 6(2) because transcription alone is not among the eight high-risk use cases, and Annex III(5)(d) covers only the evaluation and classification of emergency calls, the dispatch or priority-setting of emergency first response services, and emergency healthcare patient triage, none of which describes transcription. The system is therefore limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Yes. An AI system intended as a safety component of a robotic surgical device is high-risk under Article 6(1) because a surgical robot is a Class IIb or Class III medical device requiring notified-body conformity assessment under Article 43. Since the AI operates in a real-time control loop, Article 14 requires robust human oversight measures to allow the surgeon to override or reverse decisions. Under Article 72 and Article 73, the provider must establish post-market monitoring and report serious incidents, coordinating with the Medical Device Regulation Article 83 for layered surveillance.

This question is about the Digital Services Act (DSA), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the applicable rules.

A provider (Article 3(3)) develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity, so the provider bears the design and conformity duties of Article 16 while the deployer bears the use-phase duties of Article 26. Under Article 25 a deployer, distributor, importer, or other third party becomes a provider, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system, or modifies a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using an AI system that infers or identifies emotions of natural persons in the workplace and in education institutions, with a narrow exception for systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons. Article 50(3) requires deployers of an emotion recognition system to inform the natural persons exposed to it of the system's operation, except where the system is permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences. Outside the workplace and education settings emotion recognition is not prohibited, and where such a system interacts directly with natural persons the provider must design it to inform them they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1).
