A conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system consists of verifying that the quality management system complies with Article 17, examining the technical documentation to assess compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and verifying that the design, development process and post-market monitoring plan are consistent with the technical documentation, as set out in Annex VI for the internal-control procedure. Where the provider has not applied harmonised standards or common specifications in full, the assessment under Annex VII adds notified-body involvement: the notified body audits the quality management system, examines the technical documentation, and issues an EU technical documentation assessment certificate. For a high-risk system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I legislation, Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into that legislation's own third-party conformity assessment procedure as a single combined assessment.

Article 10 requires the provider to establish data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, ensuring that training, validation and testing datasets are relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete. The provider must examine the data for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, and may process special categories of personal data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction. Annex IV(2)(d) requires the technical documentation to describe the training methodologies and datasets used, including their provenance, scope, main characteristics, how the data was obtained and selected, labelling procedures, and data cleaning methodologies. Article 42(1) creates a presumption of compliance with the Article 10(4) data-governance requirements where the system has been trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used.

Non-compliance with the Article 50 transparency obligations is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(4). Article 50 imposes transparency duties split by actor: providers must ensure AI systems interacting with natural persons disclose their AI nature (Article 50(1)) and must mark synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable format (Article 50(2)), while deployers must inform exposed persons when operating emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems (Article 50(3)) and must label deepfakes as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)). For SMEs including start-ups, Article 99(6) sets the applicable ceiling as the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount.
The "best" restaurant is subjective and depends on your personal taste! Rome offers an incredible array of dining experiences, from traditional trattorias to innovative fine dining.

Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

Article 20(1) requires the provider to take the necessary corrective actions immediately to bring the system into conformity, withdraw it, disable it, or recall it, as appropriate, once the provider considers or has reason to consider the system is not in conformity. The Regulation does not specify a timeframe within which the market surveillance authority must allow corrective action before requiring suspension or recall, so the provider's duty to act without undue delay arises as soon as it has reason to consider non-conformity, including when the authority determines the system is high-risk. Where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 20(2) requires the provider to immediately investigate the causes and inform the market surveillance authorities and any notified body that issued a certificate. The gravity of the situation determines which corrective action is appropriate under Article 20(1), but the duty to act immediately applies in all cases of non-conformity.

A risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain.

Not automatically. Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

Article 5 prohibits eight AI practices outright: subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or socio-economic situation, social scoring leading to unjustified detrimental treatment, criminal-offence risk profiling of natural persons, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial-recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace or educational institutions, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement subject to the narrow Article 5(1)(h) exceptions.

The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

Not prohibited and not high-risk under the Annex III use cases. Article 5 prohibits eight categories of AI practice, none of which covers medical transcription. Annex III(5)(d) classifies emergency patient triage systems as high-risk but does not list transcription of doctor-patient conversations. The transcription system is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk.

No, the Regulation does not require market surveillance authorities to be provided with remote access to documentation and datasets. Article 16(k) requires the provider to demonstrate conformity with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, but it does not specify the modality of access. Article 25(2) requires the initial provider and a new provider to cooperate along the value chain, including by making available the necessary information and providing the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, but that duty runs between operators rather than to authorities.

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

High-risk only where the software is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Article 6(1) classifies a system as high-risk on those two cumulative conditions. Melanoma-detection software deployed as part of a medical device regulated under the Medical Devices Regulation or In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation would meet this route where the device itself requires third-party conformity assessment by a notified body. The system is not listed in Annex III, so Article 6(2) does not apply.

Not high-risk and not prohibited under the facts stated. Selecting patients for an experimental clinical trial is not a listed Annex III use case, so it is high-risk only where it determines access to or eligibility for essential healthcare services under Annex III(5)(a), which applies to systems used by or on behalf of public authorities, or where the biometric sorting categorises natural persons by race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, which Article 5(1)(g) prohibits. A clinical-trial selection system operated by a hospital does not evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits or services within the meaning of Annex III(5)(a), and sorting by biometric data alone does not trigger Article 5(1)(g) unless the system deduces or infers one of those six sensitive attributes. Where the system does not perform such categorisation and does not determine access to essential healthcare, it is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Yes, where the device is high-risk. A provider of a high-risk AI system must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the system under Article 72(1), actively and systematically collecting, documenting and analysing relevant data throughout the system's lifetime to evaluate continuous compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements under Article 72(2), based on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation under Annex IV as required by Article 72(3). The provider must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred under Article 73(1), immediately after establishing a causal link and not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident under Article 73(2), within 2 days in the case of a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, and within 10 days in the case of a person's death under Article 73(3) and Article 73(4).

For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

No. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk where it falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases at the time of classification, and a system that no longer performs an Annex III use case is not high-risk under that route. The classification turns on the system's current intended purpose as specified in the instructions for use, promotional materials and technical documentation (Article 3(12)), not on what it previously did.

Article 10(2)(f) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to examine training, validation and testing datasets for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination. Article 10(5) permits providers to process special categories of personal data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards and the conditions that the bias work cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data and that the special categories are subject to technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures including pseudonymisation. Article 9 requires the risk management system to be documented and to identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, to estimate and evaluate risks emerging under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and to adopt targeted risk management measures that give due consideration to the combined application of the Chapter III Section 2 requirements with a view to minimising risks more effectively. For general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, Article 55(1)(a) requires providers to perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks, and Article 55(1)(b) requires them to assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources.

No. Article 15(1) requires the provider to design and develop the high-risk system so that it achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and performs consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle. Article 9(1) requires a documented risk management system that is maintained in relation to the high-risk AI system, and Article 17(1) requires a quality management system that includes examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development. The lifecycle obligation means the provider must continue to ensure those levels are maintained, not merely confirm them once at development.
